Delirium is a sudden, serious state of mental confusion. When a person is in delirium, their mind temporarily stops working the way it normally does. They cannot think clearly, cannot focus their attention, and lose a proper sense of what is real, where they are, and what is happening around them. It is not a disease on its own — it is a state the brain enters, almost always because something else is going wrong in the body or mind.

The key word here is sudden. Delirium does not creep in slowly over months or years. It strikes fast — often within hours or a couple of days.
What Actually Happens to a Person in Delirium

To truly understand delirium, imagine your brain as a busy control room. Normally, the workers inside are alert, organized, and communicating well. In delirium, it is as if the control room suddenly loses most of its power. The workers are panicked, disorganized, and sending wrong signals everywhere. Here is what that looks like from the outside and inside:

Confusion about reality. The person may not know where they are, what day or time it is, or even who the people around them are — including close family members. They might believe they are somewhere completely different, like thinking they are at home when they are in a hospital.

Inability to focus or pay attention. They cannot hold a conversation properly. They lose track of what was just said. You might ask them a question and they start answering, then drift off mid-sentence and stare blankly — or start talking about something totally unrelated.

Disordered thinking. Their thoughts are jumbled and do not connect logically. They might say things that make no sense, jump between completely unrelated ideas, or be unable to follow simple instructions.

Hallucinations. A person in delirium often sees, hears, or feels things that are not really there. A common example is seeing insects crawling on the walls or on their skin, or hearing voices that nobody else can hear. These feel completely real to the person experiencing them.

Delusions. Along with hallucinations, they may hold false, unshakeable beliefs — for example, believing that the nurses are trying to harm them, or that they are being held prisoner.

Disorientation in time. They might believe it is a completely different year, that a deceased family member is still alive, or that events from the past are happening right now.
A Defining Feature: It Comes and Goes

One of the most important things to understand about delirium is that it fluctuates. This means the symptoms do not stay constant throughout the day. A person might seem almost normal and relatively clear-minded in the morning, then become severely confused and agitated by the afternoon, and then seem somewhat better again by evening.

This fluctuation — this "coming and going" — is actually one of the key signs that doctors look for to identify delirium. It is one of the things that makes delirium different from other mental conditions.

Delirium is also commonly worse at night, a pattern sometimes called sundowning. In the dark and quiet of the night, with fewer environmental cues like sunlight and normal activity around them, the confused person becomes even more disoriented and agitated.
The Three Types of Delirium

Delirium does not look the same in every person. It shows up in three different forms:

Hyperactive delirium is the most dramatic and recognizable form. The person becomes restless, agitated, and sometimes aggressive. They may try to get out of bed even when they shouldn't, pull out medical tubes or drips, shout, or become visibly frightened. This is the version most people picture when they hear the word.

Hypoactive delirium is the opposite and, importantly, the most dangerous — because it is often missed. Here, the person becomes unusually quiet, withdrawn, and sluggish. They stare blankly, respond very slowly, sleep excessively, and barely interact with anyone. People around them might mistake this for simply being "tired" or "weak," not realizing the brain is actually in a state of serious disruption.

Mixed delirium is a combination of both. The person swings between hyperactive and hypoactive states at different points during the day or night.
What Causes Delirium

Delirium is always caused by something — it is the brain's distress signal that the body is in trouble. Common triggers include:

Medical illness. A severe infection (like a urinary tract infection or pneumonia), especially in older adults, is one of the most frequent causes. The body's inflammatory response to infection can disrupt the brain's normal functioning.

High fever. A dangerously high temperature can directly impair brain function and trigger delirium.

Severe dehydration. When the body lacks adequate fluids and the balance of salts (electrolytes) in the blood becomes disrupted, the brain is affected.

Medications or drug interactions. Certain medications — especially sedatives, opioid painkillers, and steroids — can cause delirium. Taking multiple medications at once, or suddenly stopping certain substances, can also trigger it.

Alcohol or drug withdrawal. One of the most severe and life-threatening forms of delirium is delirium tremens, which occurs when a person who is heavily dependent on alcohol suddenly stops drinking. It can cause extreme agitation, seizures, and hallucinations.

Surgery and hospitalization. Being in an unfamiliar environment, undergoing anesthesia, experiencing pain, lack of sleep, and the stress of illness all combine to make hospitalized patients — especially the elderly — very vulnerable to delirium.

Brain injury or illness. Head injuries, strokes, and brain tumors can all directly trigger delirium.

In many cases, especially in elderly or very sick people, there is not just one cause but a combination of several factors that push the brain into delirium.
Who Is Most Vulnerable

Delirium can happen to anyone, but some people are far more at risk than others:

Elderly people are the most vulnerable. As the brain ages, it has less reserve capacity, meaning it is less able to withstand the stress of illness or medication. Something as seemingly mild as a urinary tract infection can send an elderly person into full delirium.

Critically ill patients, such as those in intensive care units (ICUs), have a very high rate of delirium — sometimes up to 80% of ICU patients experience it. The combination of serious illness, heavy medications, sleep deprivation, and an unfamiliar environment is extremely hard on the brain.

People with pre-existing cognitive problems, such as those who already have some degree of dementia, are at much higher risk.

Children with very high fevers can also experience delirium, though it tends to be milder and shorter-lived than in adults.
How Long Does Delirium Last?

Delirium is generally temporary. Once the underlying cause is identified and treated — for example, once the infection clears, the body is rehydrated, or the problematic medication is stopped — the delirium usually resolves. This can take anywhere from a few hours to several days, or sometimes weeks in more severe cases.

However, "temporary" does not mean harmless. Delirium in elderly or very ill patients is a serious medical emergency. It is associated with longer hospital stays, higher risk of complications, and in severe cases, even death if left untreated. Some older patients do not return fully to their previous level of mental clarity after a severe episode.
How Delirium Differs from Similar Conditions

Because delirium involves confusion and disrupted thinking, it is easy to mix it up with other conditions. Here is how to tell them apart:

Delirium vs. Dementia. Dementia (like Alzheimer's disease) is a slow, progressive, and permanent decline in mental function that develops over months or years. Delirium is sudden and, in most cases, reversible. The key difference is speed of onset and reversibility. Importantly, a person with dementia is much more likely to develop delirium if they get sick.

Delirium vs. Psychosis. Psychosis (such as in schizophrenia) also involves hallucinations and delusions, and the two can look very similar. The crucial difference is that delirium is always caused by a physical, medical trigger and tends to fluctuate. Psychosis arises from a psychiatric condition and does not typically fluctuate throughout the day in the same way.

Delirium vs. Plain Confusion. Ordinary confusion might mean someone is simply puzzled or cannot make up their mind. Delirium is far more severe — it is a full disruption of consciousness, attention, thinking, and often perception.
The Word Used Loosely in Everyday Life

Outside of medicine, the word delirium (and its adjective delirious) is also used in an informal, non-medical sense to describe a state of wild excitement or extreme happiness that makes a person almost unable to think straight. For example:

"The fans were in a state of delirium when their team won the championship."

"She was absolutely delirious with joy when she found out she'd got the job."

In this casual usage, the word is not describing a medical emergency — it is being used as a colorful, exaggerated way to say someone is so overwhelmed by emotion that they can barely contain themselves. The connection to the medical meaning is the idea of the mind being "overwhelmed" and losing its usual cool, rational control.
The One-Line Summary

If you had to carry just one idea in your head about the word delirium, it is this: a sudden, serious, and usually temporary state of mental confusion and disruption — caused by a physical trigger — in which a person loses clear awareness of reality, cannot focus their thoughts, and may see or believe things that are not real.
